title: Ancient Rock Cores Reveal Oxygen Was Key to Complex Life
summary:
In an open-air warehouse in tropical Darwin, Australia, dozens of trays hold cylindrical cores of rock. They were drilled from hundreds of metres below the surface by mineral exploration companies decades ago. Some of these cores, stored at the Northern Territory Geological Survey, are mudstone — a sedimentary rock formed from hardened seafloor mud. The companies had no idea the mudstone inside held fossils of microscopic organisms that lived on the seafloor of an ancient inland sea that covered much of northern Australia over 1.5 billion years ago.

A new study in Nature used these cores to tackle a huge question: what drove the rise of eukaryotes — the group of life that includes animals, plants, algae, and fungi? Eukaryotes have complex cells with a nucleus and specialized parts called organelles. Prokaryotes, like bacteria and archaea, are simpler and mostly single-celled.

Scientists know eukaryotes evolved from a merger between an archaeon and a bacterium. But they've debated whether oxygen was required from the start. Many bacteria can live without oxygen, and nearly all eukaryotes today use oxygen for survival. Yet some modern eukaryotes can thrive without it, and ancient Earth had very little oxygen.

To find answers, researchers crushed the mudstone, dissolved it, and identified over 12,000 fossils under a microscope. They also analyzed the rock's chemistry to see if oxygen was present when the sediments formed.

The results were clear: eukaryote fossils appeared only in oxygenated environments, from coastal mudflats to the open sea. Oxygen-free samples contained only simple prokaryotes. This suggests that even the oldest known eukaryotes, living 1.7 to 1.4 billion years ago, depended on oxygen.

The finding supports a long-held hypothesis that oxygen drove the evolution of complex life. It also shows how geology and fossils together can unlock our deepest origins. Next, scientists want to study even older rocks to find the very first eukaryotes.
why_it_matters: Working out whether oxygen was required for complex life shapes how scientists hunt for life on other planets — a world with no oxygen may only ever host simple microbes. It also shows how evidence buried for more than a billion years can still be recovered from drill cores and re-read by later generations of scientists.

background_read: For most of Earth's history the air and oceans held almost no oxygen. That changed when tiny photosynthetic microbes — bacteria that make food from sunlight and release oxygen — slowly filled the seas and sky with it, in what scientists call the Great Oxidation Event. Only after that did cells with a nucleus become possible.

The cores come from Darwin, a tropical city on Australia's northern coast, and they are stored by the Northern Territory Geological Survey, the government agency that keeps rock samples drilled in that region. Such cores are valuable because they give a continuous record of ancient seafloor, layer by layer, instead of scattered loose stones.

The work appeared in Nature, a science journal that has published peer-reviewed research for well over a century — meaning other experts check a study before it is printed. Nature began publishing in the 1800s and is one of the most widely read science journals in the world.

Researchers also think eukaryotes began when one simple cell absorbed another and the two merged, with the swallowed bacterium becoming the mitochondrion — the organelle that uses oxygen to release energy. That would help explain why so many eukaryotes today depend on oxygen.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — a tidy answer from unlikely samples
perspectives.description: For researchers, the result is satisfying: thousands of fossils from drilled cores match the chemistry of the rock, supporting the idea that oxygen came first. It also shows that samples collected long ago for mining can be reused to answer fundamental questions, which makes future research cheaper and faster.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — one place, one time window
perspectives.description: A sceptic would note that all the evidence comes from a single ancient inland sea in northern Australia, so it may not represent the whole planet. Missing eukaryote fossils in oxygen-free rock could also mean the fossils simply did not survive there, not that eukaryotes were absent. Until older and more widespread rocks are sampled, the case is strong but not closed.

Methodologically, the study treats rock chemistry as a proxy for an ancient environment and reads it alongside fossil abundance. That combination of geology, palaeontology and geochemistry has driven many leaps in understanding early life, because separate lines of evidence can be cross-checked against one another.

The authors want to search even older rock for the very first eukaryotes, which would pin down how closely oxygen and cellular complexity are linked. If early eukaryotes turn up in low-oxygen settings, the hypothesis would need revising. Either result would inform astrobiology, where oxygen is one of the key signals searched for on distant planets.
